sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- subagent: Delegate focused work to child agents; compose multi-child work in one workflow call.
- bg_start: Run a long-lived shell command in the background (dev servers, builds, watchers); output is captured and you're notified on exit

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use bg_start for commands expected to run long or indefinitely (servers, watch modes, long builds); use the regular bash tool for quick commands.
- bg_start processes receive no stdin — never start a command that requires interactive input.
- After bg_start, keep working; the exit result arrives automatically. Use bg_status only when you need current output before continuing.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: subagent
toolsAdded.description:
One child: {agent,task}. Independent parallel children: {workflow:"parallel",args:{tasks:[{agent,task},...]}}. Dependent multi-step work: exactly one top-level subagent workflow call with async:true; write one ```js workflow block in this reply, then call subagent({workflow:true}); children launch only inside it.
Management: {action,id?,options:{...}}; fields not in this schema go in options.
Launch agents by name and pass models as exact provider/id; an unknown agent or model returns the valid choices.
Details: guide workflows/recommended-orchestration-pattern (async, review, failure recovery), guide workflows/scripted-workflows, guide tool-reference/retained-children, guide tool-reference/external-cli-agent-profiles.

SAFETY-CRITICAL SUBAGENT GUIDANCE:
- Delegate only when the operator asked, directly or through applicable user/project instructions; size, complexity or risk alone is not authorization.
- Native async completion wakes this session: return control; do not sleep, poll or call bg_wait for it.
- One writer per cwd/worktree; isolate concurrent writers.
- After a launch or runtime failure, stop and report it; never silently switch to interactive_shell, pi -ne or another CLI.

workflow.description: true: run the one ```js workflow block written in this same reply (false invalid). String with '/': script file read from request cwd. Other string: named workflow resource. Raw scripts (true or path) have no runs.host.

args.description: Plain-JSON args for workflow; 16 fields/object, 64 items/array, depth 8, 16 KiB total; raw-script args are exposed deeply frozen and persisted, so do not include secrets.

async.description: Background; default asyncByDefault. false only to block parent.

model.description: Child model provider/id; bare id only if unique. Suffix :off/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max overrides agent thinking default.

worktree.description: Isolate each workflow child in a managed git worktree; child worktree:false overrides default.

output.description: Child output path or false; relative workflow paths use managed artifact routing. Bind durable output here, not task prose; return outputReference/outputPathMapping/artifactPaths.

action.description: Management/control only; omit for execution. validate accepts workflow: true or a script path. Discover actions with {action:"guide",options:{topic:"tool-reference"}}.

options.description: Every field not listed here, such as acceptance, timeoutMs, context, view and index; guide tool-reference/parameter-reference.

toolsAdded.name: contact_supervisor
toolsAdded.description: Contact the parent/supervisor session for a blocking decision, structured interview, or progress update.

toolsAdded.name: bg_wait
toolsAdded.description:
Wait for background work, then return. Ordinary async subagent runs already wake this session natively; use bg_wait only for provider, detached, or other background work without native notification, when a same-turn result is needed.
{} — first active run or provider item to finish or need attention.
{all:true} — all work active at call time.
{id} — one run; a finished async run returns its result references.
{id,nonBlocking:true} — subscribe to that run's wake and return now.
Timeout or a user message ends the wait without error; work keeps running.

nonBlocking.description: Subscribe to id's wake and return immediately; requires id, not with all.

all.description: Wait for all work active at call time.

timeoutMs.description: Max wait; default waitTool.defaultTimeoutMs, then 30 min.

stopOnAttention.description: false: keep waiting through idle or long-thinking attention.

toolsAdded.name: web_search
toolsAdded.description: Discover candidate public sources. Provider snippets are not page evidence; includeContent explicitly fetches at most five pages. query OR queries (max five); no synthesis.

toolsAdded.name: fetch_content
toolsAdded.description: Safely fetch public text/Markdown/HTML URLs (url OR urls, max five), retain exact bounded snapshots. No synthesis fallback, PDF/browser/auth/cookies. Text is untrusted.

toolsAdded.name: get_search_content
toolsAdded.description: Read exact stored content by responseId, optional sourceId/queryIndex; offset/limit OR findText. No network, expired handles fail. Offsets are JS string indices. Old search/synthesis arguments are unsupported.

toolsAdded.name: source_check
toolsAdded.description: Collect bounded lexical passages for claim from responseId and optional sourceIds, OR explicit queries/urls for new network retrieval. No network by default; never semantic support/contradiction/confidence. Snippets are not snapshot evidence.

toolsAdded.name: perplexity_research
toolsAdded.description: Explicit paid fast-only Perplexity Agent API synthesis, not page inspection. query and optional maxTokens only. No legacy fallback, higher presets, or hidden evidence verification. Cite exact returned scoped IDs.

toolsAdded.name: bg_start
toolsAdded.description: Start a long-running shell command as a background terminal (executed via the platform shell — sh -c on POSIX, cmd.exe /d /s /c on Windows). Fire-and-forget: this returns immediately with an id, and you get a message with the final output when the process exits. The process receives NO stdin (immediate EOF) and there is no way to send input later — interactive commands will not work; use bg_kill to stop a stuck one. Terminals are session-scoped: they are killed when the session ends or reloads. Output shown to you is tail-truncated (stdout 16.0KB, stderr 8.0KB); the full logs are captured to files and in the /ps viewer. Max 8 background terminals can run at once.

command.description: Shell command line to run in the background (sh -c on POSIX, cmd.exe /d /s /c on Windows). It receives no stdin (EOF immediately); interactive commands will not work.

title.description: Short human-readable name shown in listings and the UI

toolsAdded.name: bg_status
toolsAdded.description: Peek at a background terminal's status and current output (tail-truncated) without blocking. If the terminal already exited, this returns its final state.

toolsAdded.name: bg_list
toolsAdded.description: List all background terminals (running and settled) with pid, elapsed time, exit status, and output sizes.

toolsAdded.name: bg_kill
toolsAdded.description: Stop one or more running background terminals (SIGTERM to the whole process tree, escalating to SIGKILL). Returns each terminal's final state; already-settled ids are reported as such.

toolsAdded.name: subagent_supervisor
toolsAdded.description: Native pi-subagents supervisor channel. Use reply/pending/status to answer child subagent requests without overriding pi-intercom.

# Superhuman Email Browsing UX Specification

Desktop reference specification, excluding AI and calendar functionality.

**Status:** Evidence-backed specification with explicitly proposed interaction details. This is not a verified behavioral clone.

## Scope and interpretation

The target is the Superhuman desktop email experience shown in the supplied screenshot, cross-checked against the installed macOS application, version `1041.0.45`. The deliverable describes the experience of navigating, finding, opening, reading, and triaging existing email, rather than composing or sending it.

- **Included:** Inbox splits, conversation lists, focus and selection, conversation reading, contact context, search, folder and label browsing, native tabs and accounts, attachment viewing, manual triage, manual email reminders, and recovery.
- **Excluded:** All AI functionality, automatic classification logic, automatic summaries, generated replies, agent integrations, calendar views, availability, scheduling, meeting RSVP experiences, and event creation.
- **Boundary:** Reply, Reply All, Forward, and Compose may remain exit points from browsing. Their editor behavior, sending, templates, and signatures are not specified.
- **Manual reminders:** Included as an email snooze/triage mechanism, not as calendar functionality. Automatic reminders are excluded.
- **Existing badges:** Existing labels may be rendered as metadata. Reproducing the AI mechanism that generated an existing label is out of scope.
- **Platform:** Desktop/macOS first. Mobile gestures and responsive mobile layouts are not part of this specification.

### Evidence labels

Each requirement distinguishes recovered information from completion choices.

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `V` | Visual observation from the supplied screenshot; establishes appearance, not interaction |
| `B` | Binary-based / source-assisted observation from shipped Electron resources; static, not executed |
| `D` | Documentation-based behavior from the cited material |
| `P` | Proposed implementation contract where direct target behavior is not established |
| `U` | Unresolved fidelity question requiring a live target observation |

`D` is not equivalent to testing version 1041.0.45. Public documentation may describe a different renderer release or account capability.

### Investigation boundary

The installed Electron ASAR was inspected with the skill-pinned `rea-agents@6.5.0` runtime. Its selected source includes the native shell and production origin configuration, not a recovered authenticated mail renderer. Native tab and history code supplies limited shell evidence.

An authenticated live browsing session was not available: Comet displayed Superhuman's “Get Started Now” screen, and no Superhuman/Electron listening endpoint was found by a bounded local check. The application was not restarted, its debugging configuration was not changed, and no credentials, cookies, mail caches, or account databases were extracted.

The supplied screenshot is the only observed authenticated screen. No mail was opened, sent, archived, relabeled, or deleted during the investigation.

## Product model

The central interaction model is a sequence of actionable conversations, organized into focused inbox views, with fast transitions into individual messages. Split Inboxes are not storage folders: they represent email requiring attention, whereas folders organize stored email. (`D`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))

The three distinctions below are essential to a faithful implementation:

- **Focused versus selected:** One conversation is the current keyboard target; a separate collection can be selected for bulk actions. Superhuman documents `X`, range-extension keys, and modifier-click selection. (`D`; [Multiselect](https://new.superhuman.com/multiselect-29111))
- **Conversation versus message:** Conversation navigation uses `J`/`K`, while message navigation within a conversation uses `N`/`P`; individual messages can be expanded. (`D`; [Shortcut reference](https://nickgray.net/superhuman/), [Attachments](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005568142989-Attachments))
- **Contact pane versus message preview:** The screenshot's right pane contains sender information, not the email body. Documentation confirms that selecting an inbox conversation shows contact context in that sidebar. (`V`, `D`; [Contact Pane](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005778939789-Contact-Pane))

### Conceptual navigation hierarchy

This is a UX model, not a recovered internal schema.

```text
Native window
  Native tab
    Active email account
      Browsing context
        Inbox split | Folder | Label | Search results
          Focused conversation
          Bulk-selected conversation IDs
          Open conversation
            Focused message
            Expanded message IDs
            Active contact
            Attachment preview
```

Account identity, list context, and message identity must remain separate. A conversation can appear in more than one split when configured to also appear in Important or Other. (`D`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))

## Information architecture and layout

### Reference screen anatomy

The original image is 1028 × 1290 pixels. The geometry below uses image coordinates, not CSS pixels; device scale, capture scaling, and native window padding are unknown. All measurements are approximate. (`V`)

| Region | Reference-image geometry | Visual contract |
|---|---|---|
| Native tab/title strip | Top approximately 41 px | Thin, low-contrast strip showing view, count, and account |
| Application rail | Left approximately 40 px | Narrow persistent icon column, separated from the main surface |
| Main browsing surface | Approximately x=40–756 | Wide list area with its own top navigation |
| Contact/context pane | Approximately x=758–1027, about 270 px | Darker full-height side surface, separated by a thin vertical divider |
| Split navigation | Approximately y=76–90 | Inline split names with counts and an emphasized active split |
| First conversation | Approximately y=119–155 | Compact single-line row with focus treatment |
| Conversation rhythm | Approximately 36 px | Dense scanning rhythm; no card stack or large avatars |
| Date grouping | Between the third and fourth displayed conversations | Muted group caption with extra vertical separation |

The screenshot shows six rows in the active split, with considerable empty space below rather than stretched rows. It also shows a hamburger/menu control before the split names, compact compose/search controls after them, and utility controls at the bottom of the contact pane. (`V`)

### Main list composition

The visible column sequence is sender, optional label badges, subject, snippet, and trailing date/actions. The focused row uses a soft gray full-row background and a narrow lavender bar on the left; sender names are more visually prominent than preview text. (`V`)

```text
| focus | sender     | labels | subject      | preview text... | date/actions |
```

- **Sender column:** Fixed or constrained width; long names truncate without shifting the other rows. The screenshot contains truncated sender names. (`V`)
- **Label column:** Compact colored chips before the subject; no interpretation of the label text is required. (`V`)
- **Subject/snippet:** Occupy a single horizontal line in this reference; the preview has lower contrast and truncates at available width. (`V`)
- **Trailing area:** Unfocused rows display dates; the focused row displays several compact action icons instead. The icon identities and whether focus or pointer hover causes the replacement are not verified. (`V`, `U`)
- **Group headers:** Render chronological captions such as “Earlier this month” without turning them into selectable conversations. Exact bucket boundaries and timezone rules remain unknown. (`V`, `U`)

### Visual tokens

These are reconstruction starting values sampled from the JPEG, not recovered design-system tokens. Sampling and compression can alter apparent colors. (`V`)

| Token | Approximate reference |
|---|---|
| Main surface | `#292826` |
| Contact surface | `#1F1E1C` |
| Focus-row fill | Approximately `#474644` |
| Focus accent | Approximately `#BBA5ED` |
| Dividers | Low-contrast warm gray; about one image pixel |
| Typography | Compact sans-serif; exact family, CSS size, and weight unresolved |
| Corner treatment | Slight row rounding; avoid large rounded cards |
| Text hierarchy | Primary off-white; secondary warm gray; labels supply localized color |

Do not infer that all bold rows are unread. The screenshot does not establish the mapping between read state and text weight. (`U`)

### Reconstruction layout policy

The following fills gaps rather than asserting target behavior:

- **List mode:** Keep the rail, main list, and contact pane visible on a sufficiently wide desktop viewport. (`P`)
- **Reading mode:** Replace the main list region with the conversation reader while retaining a clear back path and contact context. Do not invent a permanent side-by-side email preview based on the screenshot. The exact target reader geometry remains unverified. (`P`, `U`)
- **Narrow desktop:** Allow subject/snippet width to contract first. Below a chosen breakpoint, collapse contact context into an explicitly opened panel rather than crushing the list; this breakpoint is a product choice, not a recovered value. (`P`)
- **Calendar removal:** Omit the screenshot's calendar rail item, calendar split, and calendar utilities from this bounded implementation. Preserve email navigation without leaving dead controls. (`P`)
- **AI removal:** Omit AI destinations, summary space, generated suggestions, and AI commands entirely. Do not reserve empty layout slots for them. (`P`)

## Inbox splits and folder navigation

### Split tabs

Split names appear across the top of the inbox; the active split is emphasized. The screenshot's active “Other” view displays a count of six. (`V`)

Split badges represent total conversations, not unread conversations. Counts disappear at zero and above 999, rather than displaying zero or an arbitrarily invented “999+” badge. (`D`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))

- **Change split:** `Tab` moves to the next split and `Shift+Tab` to the previous split. Pointer selection is an implementation contract consistent with the visible tabs; wraparound behavior is unresolved. (`D`, `P`, `U`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))
- **Empty split visibility:** Optional splits can hide when empty; Inbox, Important, and Other cannot use this setting. A hidden split remains accessible through “go to [split name].” (`D`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))
- **Overlapping membership:** A split can also show its conversations in Important/Other, depending on configuration. Do not force every split into a mutually exclusive folder model. (`D`; [Default Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005619081101-Default-Split-Inbox))

## List focus, opening, and selection

### State distinctions

A minimal implementation needs `focusedThreadId`, `selectedThreadIds`, `openThreadId`, `activeMessageId`, and `expandedMessageIds`. These are proposed model names, not extracted application identifiers. (`P`)

| State | Meaning | Rendering and action target |
|---|---|---|
| No focus | List has no active conversation | No stale contact or destructive action target |
| Focused conversation | Current keyboard target | Highlighted row; contact pane represents that conversation |
| Hovered conversation | Pointer target only | Optional action affordances; do not imply bulk selection |
| Bulk selection | Explicitly selected set | Selection markers and count; bulk actions target the set |
| Open conversation | Reader is active | Message-level navigation becomes available |

The screenshot establishes one visibly focused row. It does not establish whether hovering transfers keyboard focus, whether a first click focuses or opens, or whether opening automatically marks the thread read. (`V`, `U`)

### Proposed pointer and focus contracts

These contracts make an implementation deterministic until live fidelity tests can replace them:

- **Row click:** Open the conversation; keyboard focus alone remains available without opening it. (`P`)
- **Pointer hover:** Reveal row controls without changing the bulk-selected set or read state. (`P`)
- **Inline action click:** Act on that row and stop propagation so the reader does not open accidentally. (`P`)
- **Keyboard movement:** `J`/`K` move the conversation focus; scroll just enough to keep the focused row visible. Do not wrap at list boundaries by default. (`D` for the keys, `P` for scrolling/boundaries; [Shortcut reference](https://nickgray.net/superhuman/))
- **Open/return:** `Enter` opens the focused conversation; Back restores the exact context, focused ID, and approximate scroll position rather than resetting to the first row. (`D` for Enter, `P` for restoration; [Shortcut reference](https://nickgray.net/superhuman/))
- **Unread handling:** Focus and hover do not change read state. For an implementation, opening a loaded conversation may mark it read once; exact target timing, delay, and partial-thread rules remain unresolved. (`P`, `U`)
- **Conversation removed:** Prefer the next surviving row, then the previous row, then an empty state. Do not retain an invisible destructive-action target. (`P`)

### Bulk selection

Superhuman documents `X` to select a conversation, `Shift+J`/`Shift+K` to extend selection, and Cmd/Shift-click to select multiple conversations. (`D`; [Multiselect](https://new.superhuman.com/multiselect-29111))

For reconstruction, selection should use stable IDs rather than row positions; plain navigation should not silently select additional items. Escape should clear the selected set before leaving the list, and the UI should display how many conversations a bulk operation will affect. These exact restoration, anchor, and Escape rules are proposed. (`P`)

“Select all,” “select all from here,” and cross-page selection must not be conflated. The official shortcut sheet names both selection actions, but their precise unloaded-results semantics were not tested; do not claim a loaded-page selection covers every matching email. (`D`, `U`; [Mac shortcut sheet](https://download.superhuman.com/Superhuman%20Keyboard%20Shortcuts.pdf))

## Conversation reading

### Reader content and hierarchy

The reader must distinguish conversation-level metadata from message-level metadata. The presence of message selection, expansion, attachment selection, and per-message read-status surfaces is documented, but the full reader layout is not visible in the supplied screenshot. (`D`, `U`; [Attachments](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005568142989-Attachments), [Read Statuses](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005603745293-Read-Statuses-and-Recent-Opens-Feed))

```text
Conversation header
  Back / current browsing context
  Subject and labels
  Conversation-level triage actions
Message stack
  Collapsed message header
  Expanded message
    Sender / recipients / timestamp / details affordance
```

- **Message rendering:** Render original email content, not a generated summary. Quoted-history disclosure, remote images, sanitization policy, tracking protection defaults, and dark-mode transformations require separate validation. (`P`, `U`)
- **Next conversation:** `J`/`K` navigate conversations in the originating list, not messages within the current conversation. Preserve the search/filter/split that defined that list. (`D` for key meaning, `P` for origin preservation; [Shortcut reference](https://nickgray.net/superhuman/))

### Command palette

`Cmd+K` opens Superhuman Command; actions display shortcuts on the right, and button-hover tooltips also teach shortcuts. Documentation says shortcuts are not currently customizable. (`D`; [Keyboard Shortcuts](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/REDACTED))

For reconstruction, use a focused text input, a keyboard-navigable results list, a visibly active result, and contextual commands for the focused conversation or selected set. Enter executes the active command; Escape closes the palette and restores its origin focus. Ranking, fuzzy matching, initial suggested commands, and nested-menu behavior remain unverified. (`P`, `U`)

Remove AI and calendar commands from this bounded command catalog. This is intentional scope reduction, not a claim that those commands are absent in Superhuman. (`P`)

### Search flow

`/` starts search, and the documented flow accepts a query followed by Enter. Search covers the inbox and folders, with common operators shown in the right-hand sidebar. (`D`; [Search](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005672652301-Search), [Keyboard Shortcuts](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/REDACTED))

```text
Browsing context
  -> Search input + operator guidance
  -> Enter
  -> Results list
  -> Open conversation
  -> Back to the same results and query
  -> Back to previous browsing context
```

The transitions and preservation of result focus are proposed contracts. Autocomplete, live-result timing, result ranking, hit highlighting, and whether the list updates before Enter are unresolved. (`P`, `U`)

- **Query semantics:** Adjacent terms combine with AND; `OR` broadens the query; quoted phrases request exact matching; a leading hyphen excludes a term. (`D`; [Search](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005672652301-Search))
- **Structured criteria:** Rule-based splits document `From:`, `To:`, `Subject:`, `Bcc:`, and `Cc:` criteria, while labels can be browsed/searched using `label:`. A complete search grammar is not recovered. (`D`, `U`; [Custom Split Inbox](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005636204941-Custom-Split-Inbox), [Labels](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005736546061-Labels))
- **Result treatment:** Reuse conversation rows and keyboard navigation rather than introducing a separate card system. Retain the query while opening and closing a result. (`P`)
- **No results:** Show the query, a clear no-match message, and an immediate way to edit or clear it. Do not conflate zero results with offline incompleteness. (`P`)
- **Offline search:** Recent cached email can be searched offline; this does not establish a complete local copy of the mailbox. (`D`; [Search](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005672652301-Search))
- **Account scope:** Default reconstruction scope is the active account. Cross-account search was not established and should not be promised. (`P`, `U`)

### Context precedence

The following dispatch policy is proposed because complete target shortcut precedence was not captured:

1. Native/browser/system-reserved commands retain their expected behavior.

5. Conversation actions target an explicit bulk-selected set, otherwise the current conversation.

`Enter` and `Tab` are context-dependent. Enter can open a list conversation, commit a palette choice, or invoke Reply All inside a conversation; Tab can switch splits or navigate message links. ## State, consistency, and resilience

### Suggested state model

This model supports the specified UX without claiming a recovered implementation or backend API.

```typescript
type BrowseContext =
  | { kind: "split"; accountId: string; splitId: string }
  | { kind: "folder"; accountId: string; folderId: string }
  | { kind: "label"; accountId: string; labelId: string }
  | { kind: "search"; accountId: string; query: string };

type TabBrowseState = {
  context: BrowseContext;
  filter: null | "unread" | "starred" | "important" | "no-reply";
  orderedThreadIds: string[];
  focusedThreadId: string | null;
  selectedThreadIds: Set<string>;
  rangeAnchorThreadId: string | null;
  openThreadId: string | null;
  activeMessageId: string | null;
  expandedMessageIds: Set<string>;
  listScrollOffset: number;
  readerScrollOffset: number;
  overlay: null | "command" | "search-input" | "label" |
    "move" | "reminder" | "attachment" | "action-scope";
};
```

The four filter names are present in the official shortcut sheet; their exact combination rules and defaults are unresolved. For a bounded implementation, use one active filter at a time until live behavior establishes otherwise. (`D`, `P`, `U`; [Mac shortcut sheet](https://download.superhuman.com/Superhuman%20Keyboard%20Shortcuts.pdf))

### Required consistency invariants

All invariants here are proposed engineering contracts:

- **Stable identity:** Focus and selection attach to conversation IDs, not indexes; incoming rows cannot redirect an action to a different thread.
- **Account isolation:** Every action carries the active account identity; one account's thread IDs or selection never leak into another.
- **Independent dimensions:** Read, star, labels, inbox membership, reminder, and mute are separate state dimensions.
- **Derived views:** Update every visible view that shares a conversation, not just the list where an action started.
- **Preserved origin:** Back from a conversation restores split/folder/label/query/filter and the best surviving anchor.
- **Async safety:** Ignore stale search responses from older queries; a slow response cannot overwrite a newer results context.
- **Failure recovery:** Roll back failed optimistic changes, announce the failure, and preserve a retry path.
- **New mail stability:** Avoid shifting the focused item under the user during triage; the exact Superhuman arrival/banner policy is unknown.

### Non-happy-path states

| State | Proposed treatment |
|---|---|
| Initial loading | Preserve shell geometry and avoid displaying cached counters as confirmed fresh data |
| Empty split | Clear focus, selection, and contact context; show a split-specific completed state |
| No search matches | Keep query editable; distinguish no match from incomplete/offline results |
| Offline cached list | Allow reading cached content; make freshness/availability boundaries clear |
| Message not cached | Keep the conversation header/back path; show unavailable body with retry |
| Conversation removed elsewhere | Return to a valid list anchor; avoid a dead reader with active triage buttons |
| Mutation failure | Restore the affected state and report failure without losing navigation |
| Partial bulk failure | Distinguish succeeded and failed IDs; do not report the whole operation as successful |
| Empty contact profile | Render only known fields, with no invented enrichment |
| Attachment error | Dismiss/retry/open externally without losing the thread |
| Account authentication required | Keep local navigation state but stop claiming remote actions succeeded |

Offline recent-email search is documented; the rest of this table is a proposed resilience specification, not observed failure behavior. (`D`, `P`; [Search](https://help.superhuman.com/hc/en-us/articles/46005672652301-Search))

### Accessibility and performance targets

These are proposed acceptance targets, not measured Superhuman properties:

- **Keyboard completeness:** Every in-scope browsing operation has a discoverable keyboard route and a pointer route.
- **Semantic structure:** Expose split navigation, conversation focus/selection, expanded message state, dialogs, and attachment controls to assistive technology.
- **Visible focus:** Retain a non-color-only focus cue and explicit multi-selection state.
- **Announcements:** Announce result counts, selection counts, triage outcomes, and failures without reading the whole inbox repeatedly.
- **Contrast:** Use the sampled screenshot palette as a reference, not permission to reproduce inaccessible contrast.
- **Local response:** Aim for visible focus/selection feedback within 100 ms; measure rather than claiming parity with Superhuman.
- **Large lists:** Virtualize without invalidating keyboard navigation or screen-reader position; pagination must not silently change selection scope.

## Remaining fidelity work

The evidence supports the list composition, navigation vocabulary, many action semantics, and the native shell's role. It does not support claiming a complete recovery of the authenticated renderer.

Before calling a reconstruction behaviorally equivalent, observe the actual target on a controlled mailbox or user-approved threads:

- **List activation:** Single click versus double click, hover-to-focus behavior, initial focus, and row-action reveal trigger.
- **Read semantics:** Mark-as-read timing, partially unread threads, selection without opening, and unread-filter removal.
- **Reader geometry:** Main-panel layout, widths, message cards/headers, body rendering, quoted history, initial expansion, and scroll anchoring.
- **Navigation edges:** Split and conversation boundary wrapping, G-sequence timeout, repeated Escape, Back stack, and context restoration.
- **Selection:** X toggling, range anchors, command targeting while selected, select-all scope, and unloaded-result behavior.
- **Search:** Suggestions, ranking, all supported operators, spam/trash defaults, account scope, loading behavior, and result highlight treatment.
- **Asynchronous updates:** New-mail insertion, count updates, optimistic errors, multi-tab synchronization, and offline queues.
- **Visual details:** Exact fonts, CSS spacing, theme tokens, tooltip timing, motion, and viewport breakpoints.
- **Attachments:** Preview dismissal, chooser behavior with multiple links/files, and OS-specific download flows.

Use fresh inputs for those observations, retain before/after evidence, and compare each declared behavior rather than only matching a screenshot. No such reconstruction verification has been performed in this investigation.

## 3. Tauri: conditional recommendation and the Electron tradeoff

**Conditional fit.** Tauri 2 supplies the desktop shell primitives (native system webviews, Rust↔frontend
IPC, capabilities, tray, notifications, shortcuts, deep links, signed updates) but **not** an email
architecture, a background daemon, a complete OAuth/token solution, or a safe mail renderer.

The core tradeoff: Tauri uses the OS webview (WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on
Linux), avoiding a bundled Chromium but inheriting platform/version differences; Electron bundles
Chromium/Node for a consistent renderer baseline at the cost of footprint and heavier packaging. Neither
is automatically faster or safer; benchmark the actual workload.

Caveats: WebKit compatibility (focus, IME, typography, animation) needs early testing on real macOS
hardware — one isolated Intel Mac issue was reported in
[tauri#13141](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/13141), weak evidence of prevalence but
motivation for hardware testing. "Local-first" sync works while the process is alive, and a tray/menu-bar
mode can stay available after hiding the window, but **guaranteed sync while the app is fully quit is not
possible with Tauri async tasks alone** — that needs a separately designed helper or OS background
mechanism; decide quit-vs-hide semantics deliberately. Node-bound backend dependencies are not drop-in
(Rust backend), so a Node-heavy stack erodes Tauri's advantage. There is no official Tauri OAuth plugin;
treat community `tauri-plugin-oauth` as third-party and audit it before adoption. macOS distribution
requires code signing and, outside the App Store, notarization.

**Reconsider Electron or native if:** Chromium-consistent rendering across OS releases is a hard
requirement; product logic depends deeply on Node-only modules; guaranteed sync while quit is a core
promise; or the Rust/backend, hostile-email-security, and release-engineering work is not affordable.

## 4. Local-first architecture (proposed shape)

```
React/TS UI  →  narrow typed Tauri commands/events  →  Rust mail/sync core
                                                            │
                    SQLite (metadata + FTS5 search) ◄───────┤
                    OS secret store / Stronghold (tokens) ◄─┘
```

- **Trusted UI:** React/TypeScript; keyboard command system, list/detail, settings. Talks only through
  narrow typed commands and events.
- **Rust core:** OAuth callback handling, account/session state, provider integration (Gmail REST / IMAP /
  JMAP), MIME parsing, retryable sync coordinator, notifications, database and migrations.
- **Local store:** SQLite metadata + FTS5 search; prefer a Rust-owned DB API over exposing general SQL to
  the UI, and verify the chosen SQLite build actually enables FTS5 (Tauri's SQL plugin does not guarantee
  it). Async commands do not make a sync engine: cancellation, retries, incremental sync, conflict
  handling, backoff, and rate limits are application work.
- **Secrets:** tokens in the OS keychain (or Stronghold) — never in frontend storage or plain app config.

**Gmail full vs. incremental resync:** the sync design must handle both a full initial mailbox pull and
cheap incremental catch-up (history/sync APIs), including interruption/restart and duplicate-suppression.
Candidates document only partial answers (§2), so this must be designed explicitly.

**Durable queued actions and optimistic UI:** the desired UX is optimistic (read/archive/send reflected
instantly) with **durable local queues** so actions survive crashes, offline periods, and sync conflicts.
JakubSzwajka's `email` documents this pattern; it must be engineered deliberately (idempotent operations,
ordered retries, conflict resolution), not assumed.

**Untrusted mail rendering — the largest security obligation:** Tauri capabilities can confine a dedicated
message webview to zero privileged IPC, but they do **not** sanitize hostile HTML. Required: sanitized
HTML, scripts and forms stripped, remote images blocked or proxied by default, links opened externally
through an explicit handler, restrictive CSP, and never placing raw message markup into the privileged
app-origin DOM. Do not rely on an iframe as the security boundary (platform limits differ, notably
Linux/Android).

**OAuth flow:** authorization-code + PKCE in the system browser, random state, strict redirect/issuer
validation, one-shot loopback listener or deep-link return with a short timeout, refresh tokens never in
web storage.

**Personal vs. public OAuth verification:** personal use can qualify for a verification exception;
it does **not** inherently require leaving the OAuth consent screen in Testing status. External apps
in Testing generally receive seven-day refresh tokens for Gmail scopes; publishing status and scope
verification are separate considerations. Public distribution and server-side handling of restricted
Gmail data can introduce additional verification/security-assessment obligations. Validate the chosen
OAuth configuration rather than assuming weekly reauthentication is unavoidable. See Google's
[installed-app OAuth guidance](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/native-app) and
[restricted-scope verification guidance](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification).

## 5. Android update (post-dates the research reports)

Newer findings, more current than the reports above:

- **Tauri 2 supports Android**, but **none of the inspected Tauri clients has a documented Android
  implementation**. The upstream `JakubSzwajka/email` repository has generated Android icons only;
  those assets do **not** establish Android support.
- **Inbox Zero does document Android product support** — see the
  [mobile apps docs](https://docs.getinboxzero.com/essentials/mobile-apps) and
  [the product page](https://www.getinboxzero.com/app);
  [getinboxzero.com/android](https://www.getinboxzero.com/android) redirects to
  [the Play Store listing](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.getinboxzero.app). Its
  public repository contains mobile **server APIs** but **no mobile app directory** under `apps/` — so
  forkable Android source / self-hosted mobile compatibility is **unverified**. Do not claim the client
  source is private or absent universally; it is simply not confirmed.
- Open option: whether Android needs **custom triage behavior** vs. mere **read/reply** capability is
  **unresolved**.

**Option A — custom desktop client + existing Android Gmail app.** Use the Gmail Android app with
provider-level labels/read/archive. Provider-level state syncs across devices, but any custom local state
— snooze queues, outbox queues, triage labels outside Gmail's model — needs **explicit cross-device
design** (e.g. Gmail labels as the sync medium, or accept desktop-only semantics). Lowest build cost;
keeps Android off the critical path.

**Option B — shared Tauri/Rust core with an Android-first spike.** Validate a shared core by prototyping
on Android first: auth (system browser/PKCE), read, send, background behavior, notifications. There is
**no automatic port** — desktop shell work and Android lifecycle/background/notification constraints are
separate engineering. Highest ceiling for a unified product; highest cost and risk.

The Tauri-vs-Electron and local-first decisions should be revisited after choosing between these options.

# ADR 0001: Start with a single-account desktop email client

**Status:** Accepted — first-build direction and scope; not authorization to connect a mailbox or send mail.

## Context

Email OS's long-term direction is a composable email client whose views, signals, commands, and workflows can be adapted by users and agents. The [PRD](../../PRD.md) describes that destination, not a suitably narrow first build.

The immediate goal is a limited replacement for Superhuman. The user has confirmed that **one account on desktop is a good starting point**. The first build should therefore replace a complete everyday activity, rather than demonstrate a platform or add another tool alongside the existing client.

[Experiment 1](../../EXPERIMENT-01.md) proposes a read-only, teachable reply queue. That remains a possible later customization study, but handing users back to another client to reply would not validate the immediate replacement goal.

At the time of this ADR, the repository contained planning and static reviews. The narrower Slice 01 fixture baseline and Slice 02 read-only Gmail path are now implemented; see the slice contracts for their boundaries and `docs/development.md` for validation status. This ADR's broader provider-backed composition, sending, Gmail archive/read-state actions, search, and saved-view scope remains future work; macOS Slice 02 runtime validation is still pending.

## Decision

Build a **keyboard-first, single-account desktop client for a complete inbox-processing session**, with one small configurable-view capability.

The initial promise is:

> I can open Email OS, process my inbox, and finish ordinary replies without switching to Superhuman.

The primary loop is:

```text
Open inbox → navigate → read conversation → reply or archive → next
```

Optimize this loop for speed, predictable interaction, and trustworthy state before adding intelligent prioritization or general extensibility.

### Initial boundaries

- One connected account, not a unified multi-account inbox.
- One desktop operating system for the first developer build. macOS is approved for the Slice 02 pilot; the broader platform/runtime gate remains pending.
- Gmail REST is approved for the narrow, read-only disposable-account Slice 02 pilot. This does not authorize write scopes or broader provider capabilities; do not build a second provider merely to demonstrate abstraction.
- No custom Android surface in this build. An existing provider client remains the mobile fallback; this sequencing does not remove Android from the product vision.
- Manual operation must work without AI or external inference.
- Initial validation is personal dogfooding, not a recruited multi-user pilot.

## First-build scope

### 1. Inbox and reading

- Inbox list and conversation reader with enough message history to reply confidently.
- Predictable keyboard navigation, focus, and shortcuts for next/previous, open/back, reply, archive, and read/unread.
- Safe message rendering. A plain-text presentation is acceptable initially; HTML fidelity is not a reason to weaken isolation or sanitization.
- Visible loading, freshness, incomplete-context, and synchronization-error states.
- An explicit fallback to the provider client for unsupported operations or message formats.

### 2. Composition and sending

- Reply, reply-all, and simple new-message composition.
- Clearly displayed recipients, distinguishing reply from reply-all; no hidden recipient expansion.
- Draft persistence across application restart, including recipient and body edits.
- Basic file attachment upload/download, with explicit size/type limitations and failures. Inline editing, attachment previews, and sophisticated formatting are deferred.
- Explicit user-initiated sending, with visible operation status and failure recovery.

Drafts may initially be application-local. The interface must make that limitation clear: cross-device/provider draft synchronization is not promised.

### 3. Mailbox actions and search

- Archive and read/unread changes reflected in provider state, so ordinary mailbox state remains consistent with other clients.
- Immediate local feedback backed by durable staging and reconciliation, not optimistic success messages that hide failures.
- Basic search sufficient to find an older conversation. Provider-backed search is acceptable; a complete local full-text index is not required.
- Search results must disclose whether they cover the provider mailbox or only cached data.

### 4. One configurable view

Provide one additional saved queue defined by a bounded, declarative filter over sender, domain, or existing provider labels, with a stable default order. It must reuse the ordinary reader, composer, and mailbox commands.

- A small manual editor is sufficient; no natural-language authoring is required.
- Keep the full inbox accessible. Filtering must not silently archive, relabel, or hide mail from the provider inbox.
- Store the definition locally for the first build; do not imply it follows the user to mobile.
- If referenced data is not loaded, disclose the view's coverage.

This is a small test of the composable direction, not a general rules engine. Do not add new provider permissions or mutation capabilities merely to support view configuration.

## Architecture constraints

Preserve a few internal boundaries without committing to a public SDK:

1. **Mail integration and local state:** own credentials, synchronization, message identity, caching, and reconciliation outside UI components.
2. **Views:** select and order conversations from available data; they do not execute mailbox mutations.
3. **Commands and execution:** route UI actions through one typed boundary responsible for validation, durable operation state, concurrency, and recovery.
4. **Presentation:** consume those interfaces for the default inbox and the configurable view.

Use local data for responsive navigation where available. Opening a cached conversation must not require a fresh provider request to render its cached content.

Persist drafts and staged operations across restart. Cached reading and draft editing should remain usable without a connection; full offline mailbox coverage and offline search completeness are not required. Distinguish local, pending, and provider-confirmed state.

A send with an ambiguous remote outcome must enter an explicit **outcome unknown** state and be reconciled rather than blindly retried. Do not promise universal exactly-once sending or provider-side undo after delivery.

Synchronization is required while the application is running. Guaranteed synchronization, sending, or timer execution while the application is fully quit is out of scope. Hide-versus-quit behavior must be documented.

Framework, storage implementation, shell, and reuse strategy require separate technical decisions. This ADR does not select Tauri, Electron, Rust, React, or either reviewed fork.

## Safety and release gates

Narrow scope does not justify weaker mail integrity or privacy.

Before primary-mailbox dogfooding, use synthetic fixtures and a disposable account to validate:

- Authentication refresh/revocation and secure credential storage.
- Hostile-message rendering, blocked active content, and blocked automatic remote-resource loading.
- Recipient integrity for reply, reply-all, and new messages.
- Thread/context correctness and attachment handling.
- Interrupted synchronization, recovery after restart, and changes made in another client.
- Draft recovery and pending/failed mailbox mutations after connection loss.
- Concurrent send attempts and ambiguous-send recovery without blind replay.
- Search/view coverage and unsupported-message fallbacks.

Do not put mailbox content or credentials into routine diagnostic logs. Any reused code implicated by the [email](../../security/email-review.md) or [Pebble](../../security/pebble-review.md) reviews must be fixed and tested, or demonstrated to be outside reachable paths. Those static reviews are not runtime safety certifications.

## Explicit non-goals

- Superhuman feature parity or a polished public launch.
- Multiple accounts, multiple providers, or a custom mobile client.
- AI classification, generated replies, or agent-authored configuration.
- Public plugins, arbitrary extension code, a marketplace, or stable external APIs.
- Follow-up automation, reminders, scheduled send, sophisticated snooze, or background execution while quit.
- Application-owned state replication across devices.
- Complete offline mailbox search, advanced rich-text editing, attachment previews, or inline attachment composition.
- Recruitment, billing, or the customization pilot described in Experiment 1.

## Acceptance and evaluation

After the safety gates pass, dogfood the build for **five working days**.

The target is completing ordinary desktop inbox-processing sessions in Email OS. Keep the existing client available and record every fallback, including its reason and whether it blocked completion.

Evaluate:

- **Completion:** Can ordinary read/reply/archive sessions finish here? Which missing capabilities force a switch?
- **Interaction:** Does navigation remain responsive, focus predictable, and the primary loop usable without repeated mouse intervention?
- **Trust:** Do drafts survive restart, mailbox changes converge, and failures remain visible? Any silent data loss, unintended recipient, or duplicate-send defect blocks progression.
- **Composition:** Can the additional queue be changed declaratively without a new UI/core code path?

The five-day window is an evaluation period, not a build-time estimate. A high fallback rate is evidence to revise the scope, not a reason to hide unsupported cases. Prioritize the next slice from observed blockers rather than feature count or the breadth of the PRD.

## Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why not first |
|---|---|
| Read-only teachable queue | Tests customization but cannot replace a complete email-processing session. |
| Reply-only workspace | A credible smaller fallback if the client scope proves too large, but leaves general inbox triage elsewhere. |
| Configurable split inbox as the main feature | Useful later; puts configuration before proving the basic read/reply/archive experience. |
| Follow-up-oriented client | Adds timers, reply detection, and execution ownership before the underlying mail loop is trustworthy. |
| Full composable-platform MVP | Too many independent risks: mail correctness, extension contracts, agent authority, automation, and multi-device state. |

## Consequences

**Benefits:** Delivers direct personal utility, validates the mail foundation against real work, and retains a modest path toward composable workflows. Avoids making AI or platform infrastructure a dependency of ordinary email use.

**Costs:** Less differentiated initially, requires consequential send/sync engineering earlier than the read-only experiment, and deliberately leaves mobile and advanced workflows in other clients. Keyboard interaction quality becomes a core acceptance criterion rather than later polish.

**Sequencing change:** This client slice takes priority over Experiment 1. The experiment remains a proposed later study of whether personalization adds value once the application can complete the work itself. The PRD remains the long-term direction; this ADR governs the narrower first build.

**Revisit when:** Dogfooding reveals a missing capability that prevents meaningful replacement, single-account desktop use is insufficient, or implementation effort warrants narrowing to the reply-only alternative. Change the ADR explicitly rather than silently expanding scope.

# Development guide

This repository contains two deliberately separate native profiles: the durable
synthetic fixture slice (Slice 01) and an explicit Gmail profile built in stages.
Slice 02 adds system-browser OAuth/PKCE, a macOS Keychain credential store,
bounded inbox caching, and background sync. Slice 03 adds opt-in, durable Gmail
archive/unarchive and explicit read/unread actions; Gmail remains read-only until
the user explicitly requests the broader Google `gmail.modify` permission.
Slice 04 adds a local-only plain-text composer and durable draft recovery, but
still does not send/delete mail or expose arbitrary labels. Opening a message
never marks it read. The browser preview remains synthetic and in-memory. See
the slice contracts for individual acceptance scope.

**Browser preview (in-memory, not durable):** `mise run dev:web`, then open the
printed localhost URL. The disclosure banner identifies the labelled fake client;
there is no real OAuth or mailbox access in browser preview.

**Native fixture mode (default):** `mise run dev:native`. This opens the synthetic
fixture profile under `<app_data_dir>/fixture-profile`; local drafts are stored
separately beneath `<app_data_dir>/fixture-profile/local-drafts`. The fixture
provider's optional demo behavior is selected with
`EMAIL_OS_FAKE_PROVIDER=paused|reject|success` (default: success). Profile locks
reject a second writer to the same mail or draft profile.

**Explicit native Gmail mode:** launch with `EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail`; it uses the
separate `<app_data_dir>/gmail-profile`, never the fixture database. Local drafts
are in the separate `<app_data_dir>/gmail-profile/local-drafts` profile; disconnect
retains those drafts on this device for the same account after reconnect. Set the
Google client environment before launching:

```sh
EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail \
EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID='your-desktop-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com' \
EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET='optional-desktop-client-secret' \
mise run dev:native
```

The client secret is optional. It belongs only in the local launch environment,
not source control, frontend state, logs, or a shell history copied into a report.
Initial connection requests only `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly`.
Missing/blank client ID shows `Not configured` in Gmail mode; it does not fail app
startup or fall back to the fixture. Unsupported Keychain platforms fail closed.
Mailbox controls stay disabled until the user selects **Enable mailbox actions**
and Google returns a verified modify grant for the same authenticated account.
That upgrade requests `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify`; Google's
scope is broader than this app's implemented archive/unarchive and read/unread
commands and can authorize other mailbox changes (including sending or deleting
mail). The app does not provide those broader actions, arbitrary labels, or a
composer. Denial or cancellation leaves the read-only account and cached reading
available.

### Google Desktop OAuth setup (disposable account only)

For the explicitly approved Mac smoke path, use a dedicated Google Cloud project
and disposable Gmail account, not a primary/personal mailbox:

1. Enable the **Gmail API** in the project.
2. Configure the OAuth consent screen and add the disposable account as a test
   user when the app is in **Testing** status.
3. Create an OAuth client of type **Desktop app**. Put its client ID in
   `EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`; the optional client secret goes only in
   `EMAIL_OS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` in the launch environment.
4. Confirm initial connection requests only `gmail.readonly`. The separate
   **Enable mailbox actions** flow requests Google's broader `gmail.modify` scope
   only after explicit user opt-in; do not add any other Gmail scopes.
5. On first use, review the macOS Keychain access prompt and allow the app to use
   its Gmail credential item. Credential-storage failures are visible and fail
   closed; there is no plaintext fallback.

Google OAuth clients left in Testing can issue refresh tokens that expire after
seven days for these Gmail scopes. Plan for a fresh sign-in during testing; this
is not a reason to log or persist tokens elsewhere. A terminal-launched Tauri
process inherits that terminal's environment. Finder-launched apps generally do
not inherit the shell's exported variables; if configuration appears missing,
use the documented launch environment for the app rather than silently selecting
fixture mode. Never paste secrets into the UI or a bug report.

Disconnect removes credentials from this app's Keychain item and clears the
local Gmail profile/cache. It is a **local disconnect**, not a promise to revoke
the Google grant or revoke tokens remotely; revoke authorization through the
Google account controls separately if required.

### Gmail sync pacing and rate limits

The disposable-account diagnostic observed HTTP 403 `rateLimitExceeded` after
~60 rapid thread reads, so discovery is paced for read-only Gmail quotas:
`threads.list` discovery pages request 25 threads (the overall disclosed cap
stays 100 conversations), consecutive Gmail API reads are separated by a
100 ms minimum interval whose wait aborts promptly on cancellation, and a
mid-page failure commits the threads already fetched (the page token is not
advanced), so a rate-limit retry or restart resumes from durable progress
instead of re-fetching saved threads. HTTP 403 is classified by bounded
structured Google error reasons: only genuine quota rejections (e.g.
`rateLimitExceeded`, `userRateLimitExceeded`, `dailyLimitExceeded`,
`quotaExceeded`, `resourceExhausted`) surface as `rate_limited`; permission
denials and unclassifiable bodies surface as the generic provider error. Raw
response bodies, messages, mailbox data, or URLs with IDs are never logged or
exposed over IPC.

- Verify fixture is the default, `EMAIL_OS_MODE=gmail` is explicit, and missing
  client ID reports `Not configured` without fixture rows.
- Connect, complete the system-browser OAuth/loopback callback, cancel once, and
  verify cancellation is recoverable; confirm Keychain credentials survive an
  app restart without exposing them.
- Complete bounded initial discovery, inspect plain-text content and unsupported
  content disclosures, and verify archive controls/shortcuts remain absent until
  the separate explicit Slice 03 permission upgrade is enabled.
- Quit, disable network, relaunch, and read cached conversations offline; restore
  network and sync. Change/archive/delete a thread using the external disposable
  Gmail client and confirm catch-up updates the local inbox without skipping the
  expired-cursor recovery path.
- Disconnect and confirm local cache/credentials are cleared while understanding
  that Google authorization itself is not remotely revoked.

No real-account OAuth, Gmail network, or macOS Keychain behavior was tested in the
Linux integration VM. The operator's earlier Slice 01 validation and prior Slice 02
Mac validation are separate gates; neither substitutes for the new Slice 03
consent, mutation, recovery, and external-change checks.

# Slice 04: plain-text composer and durable local-only drafts

Status: approved implementation contract. The operator chose this slice while testing Slice 03. Development initially stacked on `a6e2acf` for profile/credential compatibility without changing the tested branch. After Slice 03 was merged upstream, the unpublished `feat/local-drafts` branch was rebased onto main `b45c7a6`; that upstream tree differs from the reviewed base only by a Cargo.toml trailing newline. No Slice 03 branch or commit was modified by this work. Do not change OAuth, mutation dispatch/ordering, or sending. No accounts, actual credentials/mail, OS packages, or cloud provisioning in this VM. Parent owns commits/publication; children do not spawn agents or commit/push/publish.

## Scope

New-message and **Reply** plain-text composition, explicit editable To/Cc/subject/body, durable revision-checked autosave, draft list/reopen/discard, save failures/conflicts without silent overwrite, normal native close/quit flush. No Send button/action/IPC, outbox, provider draft synchronization, attachments, HTML/rich text, AI, new OAuth scopes, or automatic read/archive. Reply-all/Bcc and signatures/automatic quoted bodies are deferred; Reply never copies To/Cc implicitly.

Drafts are explicitly local to this profile/device. Browser preview remains synthetic, in-memory and non-durable (never call its acknowledgement durable). Only acknowledged saves survive a crash/force quit; normal close/quit must flush the latest buffer and stay open on failure/conflict. Checkpoint: start a reply, edit recipients/subject/body, normally quit/restart, recover the exact text; interrupted/stale saves cannot silently overwrite newer edits.

## Persistence/account/lifecycle policy

Use concrete separate `local-drafts/drafts.db` below the existing selected fixture/Gmail profile, with its own OS profile lock and short FULL/WAL transactions; do not couple to the 100-conversation cache or mutation worker. All account IDs/draft IDs/request keys are scoped and parameterized. Local drafts remain usable offline/auth-expired when cached account identity exists; no Gmail modify permission is needed. Native derives the active account from backend status, never trusts an account object from JS.

Disconnect RETAINS local drafts, unlike mail-cache/operation cleanup. Warn clearly: local drafts remain on this device, accessible after reconnecting the same account; confirmed remote actions are not undone. Before UI-initiated disconnect/account transition, flush/close the active editor; failure prevents the transition and preserves the buffer. Other account data must never appear in the new account. Native serializes draft operations and disconnect with a lifecycle/session gate; if a reply metadata read requires network, release the gate during the read and recheck account/session epoch before draft creation. Never hold SQLite/control locks during network. Query/save/delete for a DraftRef not matching the active account are rejected. Same-account reauth does not invalidate drafts. No silent draft deletion on cache eviction, auth failure or restart.

The core stores incomplete/invalid recipient text AS TYPED because autosave must not lose partially edited addresses. Save is not recipient validation or send readiness. No trim, Unicode normalization, silent address expansion, subject/body rewriting, or sending. Bound To/Cc to 16 KiB each, subject to 4 KiB, body to 1 MiB UTF-8; surface invalid_request rather than truncate. List returns summaries only (all small-slice drafts; no silent truncation), not bodies. Discard is revision-checked and explicitly confirmed in UI. Request tombstones/receipts contain no body; late saves after deletion do not resurrect a draft. No secure-erasure guarantee is implied by record deletion.

## Frozen wire contract (Rust-owned/generated)

Add types under `mail_core::drafts::types` and generated exports. CamelCase fields, snake_case discriminants, opaque string IDs/ISO UTC times, u32 revisions start at 1:

- `ReplyContext = { sourceMessageId: string; fromMailbox: string; replyToMailboxes: string[] | null; messageId: string; references: string[] }`. null replyTo means the header was absent, not malformed. Optional `Conversation.replyContext?`; absence means metadata unavailable. Existing reading remains unaffected.
- `DraftRef = { accountId: string; draftId: string }`.
- `DraftContent = { to: string; cc: string; subject: string; bodyText: string }` (raw editor fields, unvalidated for sending).
- `DraftSource = { kind: 'new_message' } | { kind: 'reply'; conversation: ConversationRef; sourceMessageId: string }`.
- `DraftReplyLink = { conversation: ConversationRef; sourceMessageId: string; messageId: string; references: string[] }`; immutable, captured from trusted cached/refreshed metadata on create.
- `Draft = { ref: DraftRef; revision: number; createdAt: string; updatedAt: string; content: DraftContent; source: DraftSource; replyLink: DraftReplyLink | null }`.
- `DraftSummary = { ref: DraftRef; revision: number; updatedAt: string; subject: string; to: string; source: DraftSource }`.
- `DraftReceipt = { ref: DraftRef; revision: number; savedAt: string }`; returned only after commit.
- `DraftDeleteReceipt = { ref: DraftRef; deletedAt: string }`.
- `CreateDraft = { requestId: string; source: DraftSource; initialContent: DraftContent | null }`. null means blank/prefilled defaults; initialContent permitted ONLY for new_message (e.g. explicit Save as new local draft after conflict).
- `SaveDraft = { ref: DraftRef; expectedRevision: number; requestId: string; content: DraftContent }`.
- `DeleteDraft = { ref: DraftRef; expectedRevision: number; requestId: string }`.
- `MailError` adds `draft_conflict { currentRevision: number }` and `reply_unavailable`; reuse not_found/invalid_request/auth_required/storage_unavailable/profile_in_use/request_id_conflict. Never put content/addresses/headers in routine logs or errors; DraftContent Debug is redacted.

IPC: `list_drafts` (no args -> DraftSummary[]), `get_draft` ({ ref } -> Draft), `create_draft` ({ command } -> DraftReceipt), `save_draft` ({ command } -> DraftReceipt), `delete_draft` ({ command } -> DraftDeleteReceipt). `drafts_changed` is an empty change hint; subscribe before initial list, refetch on focus/reconnect/events, never overwrite an active dirty buffer from a background query.

## Core API / revision and retry semantics

`DraftCore::open(profile_dir: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self,MailError>` opens the dedicated local-draft subprofile supplied by shell (the argument is already `<selected-profile>/local-drafts`). Cloneable/thread-safe, no worker/network/Tauri dependency. Methods:

- `list_drafts(account: &AccountInfo)` -> Vec<DraftSummary>
- `get_draft(account: &AccountInfo, ref: &DraftRef)` -> Draft
- `lookup_create_receipt(account: &AccountInfo, command: &CreateDraft)` -> Option<DraftReceipt> (lets shell dedup before fetching reply metadata)
- `create_draft(account: &AccountInfo, command: &CreateDraft, conversation: Option<&Conversation>)` -> DraftReceipt
- `save_draft(account: &AccountInfo, command: &SaveDraft)` -> DraftReceipt
- `delete_draft(account: &AccountInfo, command: &DeleteDraft)` -> DraftDeleteReceipt

All methods return Result<_,MailError>. AccountInfo is supplied by trusted native adapter/test, not UI. Verify ref/source account matches it. Create/save/delete atomically persist content/revision/request mapping before ACK. Request-key lookup precedes deriving reply defaults/current revision/existence checks: same account+key+identical command returns the exact original receipt even after newer saves/deletion; different payload conflicts. Hashes may fingerprint bounded JSON (sha2 already available). Request keys max128 bytes; no inferred success. Revision stale => draft_conflict(currentRevision) with no write; overflow fails closed. Save never creates missing drafts. Delete never races a stale save into resurrection. IDs opaque, random UUIDs acceptable; migration never reseeds/reset existing drafts. Storage/schema errors visible, no log-and-ignore.

## Safe reply preparation and cache metadata

Reply targets the explicitly displayed latest message (`sourceMessageId` captured on click), not a silently substituted message. Real replies require complete plaintext context, a matching source ID, non-retained current cache (retainedSnapshotAt absent), valid From/Reply-To and RFC Message-ID/reference metadata. Default deny if unavailable/ambiguous. Never infer a recipient from display names. Parse raw address grammar before decoding words, reject groups/ambiguous malformed headers. Reply-To header absent -> From mailbox; present but invalid/empty -> unavailable, not fallback. Canonical single-mailbox strings only; bounded <=20 reply-to recipients, each <=254 bytes, no CR/LF/controls. Ignore display names for prefill. Dedup mailboxes case-insensitively and exclude the known primary account address; if none remain, deny. Do not infer aliases/dot/plus equivalence; recipient review remains explicit. Replies to the account's own latest sent message are unsupported in this slice. Cc starts empty. Subject gets one Re: prefix; body blank, not automatically quoted.

RFC Message-ID must be one bounded `<id@domain>` token without controls/whitespace/injection; References (or single valid In-Reply-To if References absent) bounded to 100 IDs /16 KiB total, append source Message-ID once without silently truncating. Core independently validates before persisting DraftReplyLink; it is immutable on save and survives source cache eviction. Invalid/missing headers never break ordinary reading.

Metadata owner adds optional cached reply-context JSON additively to the Gmail conversation cache and fixture reader, with absence on legacy rows. Fixture uses the real fixture primary `you@fixture.emailos`, synthetic RFC IDs and explicit absent Reply-To; native/fake fixture account email must agree.

Legacy rows need a practical readonly enrichment path: add `GmailCore::load_reply_context(ref: &ConversationRef, source_message_id: &str) -> Result<Conversation,MailError>` as a narrow cached/read helper. No body/label/cursor/operation updates, no mutation-worker scheduling change. Current cached get_conversation remains network-free. Backend checks create receipt first; no metadata RPC for a duplicate create. Native Window CloseRequested and RunEvent ExitRequested intercept normal close/quit until current dirty/pending saves ACK. Add `AppCloseRequest = { requestId: string }`, event `app_close_requested` carrying it, and narrow commands `get_app_close_request` (-> AppCloseRequest|null), `complete_app_close` ({ requestId }, void), `cancel_app_close` ({ requestId }, void). Gate completion authorizes final app.exit, whose final Exit stops existing mail worker as before.

Native transport listens before querying pending close to recover a missed early hint; dedup repeated request IDs. On close, freeze/flush the latest active buffer (drain one-in-flight/coalesced saves), then complete only the still-current request. On failure/conflict keep the window/buffer open, cancel that close request and show the error; no forced discard or unacknowledged 'saved' claim. No cancel/edit after final completion dispatch. Browser preview fake models the protocol but never claims persistence; beforeunload warns when dirty/pending, no durable reload promise. Force quit/OS crash before ACK is explicitly not guaranteed.
